question.prompt: Two of the altitudes of the scalene triangle \(ABC\) have length \(4\) and \(12.\) If the length of the third altitude is also an integer, what is the biggest it can be?

solutions.explanation:
Each side and its corresponding altitude give the same triangle area, so we can relate the sides without finding any angles. Let \(h>0\) be the third altitude, and let \(a,b,c\) be the sides opposite the altitudes \(4,12,h\), respectively. If the area is \(K>0\), then
\[
4a=12b=hc=2K.
\]
Consequently,
\[
a=3b,\qquad c=\frac{12b}{h}.
\]
Since \(a>b>0\), the strict triangle inequalities require
\[
a-b<c<a+b.
\]
Substituting the expressions above gives
\[
2b<\frac{12b}{h}<4b.
\]
Dividing by \(b>0\) and multiplying by \(h>0\), we obtain
\[
2h<12<4h,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad 3<h<6.
\]
The only integer candidates are \(4\) and \(5\). If \(h=4\), then \(c=a\), which would make the triangle isosceles rather than scalene.

To check that \(h=5\) is attainable, consider side lengths \(15,5,12\). They are distinct, and the largest side satisfies \(15<5+12\), so they form a nondegenerate scalene triangle. By the area formula, its corresponding altitudes have ratio
\[
\frac1{15}:\frac15:\frac1{12}=4:12:5.
\]
Scaling the triangle so that the altitude opposite side \(15\) becomes \(4\) makes the other two altitudes \(12\) and \(5\). Thus the largest possible integer third altitude is \(\boxed{5}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
solutions.title: Relate the altitudes through the common area
